title: UROFACIAL SYNDROME 1
alt_titles: FACIAL PALSY, PARTIAL, WITH URINARY ABNORMALITIES
INVERTED SMILE AND OCCULT NEUROPATHIC BLADDER

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that urofacial syndrome-1 (UFS1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the HPSE2 gene on chromosome 10q24.

checks.claim: Urofacial syndrome-1 (UFS1) is caused by homozygous mutation in the HPSE2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygous exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations in five further unrelated families confirmed HPSE2 as the causative gene for UFS.
checks.explanation: The paper reports homozygous HPSE2 mutations as the cause of UFS.

checks.claim: The HPSE2 gene is located on chromosome 10q24.
checks.evidence_quote: Previously, we localized the defective gene for the urofacial syndrome (UFS) to a region on chromosome 10q24 by homozygosity mapping. We now report evidence that Heparanse 2 (HPSE2) is the culprit gene for the syndrome.
checks.explanation: The disease gene was mapped to 10q24, and HPSE2 was identified as that gene.

paragraphs.text: Urofacial syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. Its main features are an unusual 'inverted' facial expression, in which affected people appear to be crying when they try to smile, and failure of the urinary bladder to empty completely, without anatomic bladder outflow obstruction or overt neurologic damage (Daly et al., 2010; Derbent et al., 2009). Patients have enuresis, urinary tract infection, hydronephrosis, and voiding dysfunction caused by neurogenic bladder (Wang et al., 1997). Reflux of infected urine to the upper renal tract can damage the kidneys and lead to renal failure (Daly et al., 2010).

paragraphs.text: Elejalde (1979) described 7 patients (4 females and 3 males) from 3 unrelated families. One family was consanguineous (first cousins). The patients had a peculiar facies and peculiar gestures when smiling and crying. Their urinary findings were hydronephrosis, hydroureter, intravesical stenosis of the ureter, abnormal caliber of the urethra in the prostatic and membranous portions, urethral valves, and an abnormal bladder with trabeculation and diverticula. The diverticula were associated with severe hypertrophy of the mucosa with sclerotic changes. Elejalde (1979) noted that the peculiar facies allows early recognition of the condition.

paragraphs.text: Between 1965 and 1986, Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) saw 36 children who had enuresis and urinary tract infection together with 'inversion' of facial expression when laughing. In all cases, urologic work-up showed characteristic findings of mild neuropathic bladder, and most patients had severe urinary tract damage. About two-thirds of the patients also had moderate to severe constipation. The authors suggested that individuals with 'inversion' of facial expression should have a urologic evaluation.

paragraphs.text: Wang et al. (1997) performed a genome screen in 20 selected patients from Colombia, combining homozygosity mapping with DNA pooling against 1 patient pool and 3 control pools of unaffected relatives. After 36 randomly chosen markers had been analyzed, they found that D10S677 was linked to and associated with UFS. Patients showed a significant excess of homozygosity at this marker compared with unaffected relatives (P less than 10(-6)). Fine mapping with 10 additional markers covering a 22-cM region showed that all 31 patients were homozygous at 2 closely linked markers, D10S1726 and D10S198, which lie about 5 cM telomeric to D10S677. Only 12% of unaffected relatives were homozygous at both markers (P less than 10(-19)). Recombination events in several patients placed the UFS gene within a 1-cM interval between D10S1433 and D10S603 on chromosome 10q23-q24.

paragraphs.text: Several studies supported genetic homogeneity of urofacial syndrome. Wang et al. In a French family, Chauve et al. (2000) found haplotypes compatible with the same critical region, which favored genetic homogeneity. Wang et al. (2003) concluded that the same gene on chromosome 10q is responsible for the disorder in all UFS patients from multiple ethnic groups.

paragraphs.text: Pang et al. (2010) identified loss-of-function mutations in the HPSE2 gene in all patients with urofacial syndrome originating from Colombia, the United States, and France. HPSE2 encodes a 592-amino acid protein. It contains a domain with sequence homology to the glycosyl hydrolase motif of the heparanase (HPSE) gene. The authors suggested that HPSE2 may be important for the coordinated action of muscles involved in facial expression and urine voiding.

paragraphs.text: Within an autozygous region on chromosome 10q23-q24, Daly et al. (2010) identified a 10-kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of the HPSE2 gene in an individual with urofacial syndrome. In 5 further unrelated families, they found homozygous exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations in HPSE2, confirming it as the causative gene. HPSE2 was expressed in the fetal and adult central nervous system and in bladder smooth muscle.

paragraphs.text: Elejalde (1979) and Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) both emphasized that the characteristic facial expression allows early recognition of the disorder and should prompt urologic evaluation. Garcia-Minaur et al. (2001) and Derbent et al. (2009) noted that the diagnosis may be missed because the urinary problems vary and the facial grimacing goes unrecognized. Derbent et al. (2009) recommended considering the syndrome in any patient with dysfunctional voiding, particularly in countries with high rates of consanguineous marriage.

checks.claim: Elejalde (1979) and Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) emphasized that the characteristic facial expression of urofacial syndrome allows early recognition of the disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: The peculiar facies allows early recognition of the condition

checks.claim: Elejalde (1979) and Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) emphasized that the characteristic facial expression of urofacial syndrome should prompt urologic evaluation.
checks.evidence_quote: should prompt urological evaluation of individuals with "inversion" of facial expression.
checks.explanation: Stated directly for Ochoa and Gorlin.

checks.claim: Garcia-Minaur et al. (2001) and Derbent et al. (2009) noted that the diagnosis of urofacial syndrome may be missed because the urinary problems vary and the facial grimacing goes unrecognized.
checks.evidence_quote: It is likely that they may be missed because of variability of the urinary problems and failure to recognize the characteristic facial grimacing.
checks.explanation: The abstract supports the part attributed to Garcia-Minaur et al. The Derbent et al. (2009) part depends on that other paper and is not addressed here.

checks.claim: Derbent et al. (2009) recommended considering urofacial syndrome in any patient with dysfunctional voiding, particularly in countries with high rates of consanguineous marriage.
checks.evidence_quote: Physicians should keep this syndrome in mind for any patient who presents with dysfunctional voiding, particularly in countries with high rates of consanguineous marriage.
